opus-5.5.text:
I think the biggest change is going to be in where developers spend their time. For most of the history of software, a huge fraction of the job has been the mechanical act of translating an idea in your head into syntax the computer understands: looking up APIs, writing boilerplate, wiring things together, chasing down off-by-one errors. Coding systems are getting really good at exactly that layer, and I think that part of the job is going to shrink dramatically.

What that leaves is the part that was always the hard part, which is figuring out what to build and specifying it clearly. When you work with these systems day to day, you notice pretty quickly that the bottleneck shifts from "can I write this code" to "do I actually know what I want, and can I communicate it precisely enough?" So I think the skills that become more valuable are things like system design, breaking a problem down into well-scoped pieces, writing good specs, and, maybe most importantly, evaluation: being able to look at what came back and judge whether it's actually correct, secure, and maintainable.

The other shift is that developers start to look a bit more like managers or tech leads, even early in their careers. Instead of writing every line yourself, you're delegating tasks to agents, reviewing their work, and deciding when to step in. That's a different muscle. Some people find it really natural and some people find it frustrating, because the satisfaction of writing the code yourself goes away a little bit.

I'd also push back on the idea that this means fewer software engineers. Historically, every time we've made software cheaper to produce, we've ended up producing a lot more of it. There's an enormous backlog of software that never got written because it wasn't worth the engineering cost: internal tools, small automations, niche products. As the cost drops, a lot of that becomes viable. So I expect the nature of the work to change a lot, but the demand for people who can think clearly about building systems is probably going to go up, not down.

r001.rationale: The response predicts that mechanical coding work will shrink and that developers will delegate tasks to agents, but it does not clearly predict that AI systems will write the vast majority of software code.

r002.rationale: It says the bottleneck will shift to figuring out what to build and communicating it precisely, and names writing good specs as a more valuable skill.

r003.rationale: It identifies evaluation as a more valuable skill and describes judging whether AI-produced work is correct, secure, and maintainable.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the honest answer is that it's already changed a lot, and I think people underestimate how far along we are. If you look at the way a lot of engineers at frontier labs, or really at any company that's leaned into this, work today, they're not typing most of the code anymore. They're describing what they want, reviewing what comes back, and steering. The agent is doing the keystrokes.

But I think the more interesting question is what happens to the shape of the job, not just the speed of it. And the way I'd frame it is that the bottleneck moves. For most of the history of software, the bottleneck was implementation. You had an idea, and the hard part was turning that idea into working code. That's getting dramatically cheaper. So the bottleneck shifts upstream to things like: do you actually know what you want to build? Can you specify it clearly? Can you evaluate whether the thing that came back is correct? And it shifts downstream to things like verification, testing, and understanding systems you didn't personally write.

That last one I think is a big deal. If an agent writes ten thousand lines of code for you in an afternoon, you now have a code comprehension problem, not a code generation problem. So I think a lot of the craft of being a good engineer going forward is going to look more like being a good tech lead or a good reviewer. You're setting direction, you're designing the architecture, you're deciding what the invariants are, you're building the tests and the evals that let you trust what's being produced, and you're developing taste about when the model's output is subtly wrong.

The other thing I'd say is that the unit of work changes. Right now most people still interact with these systems in a pretty synchronous way. You ask, you wait, you look. I think we're moving toward a world where you have multiple agents running in parallel, working on different things over hours, and your job is more like managing a team than pair programming with one assistant. That's a pretty different skill set, and I don't think our tools or our workflows have caught up to it yet.

And then the thing I'm most uncertain about is what happens to the number of people doing this. One view is that software gets so cheap that the demand explodes, and you have way more people building things who never would have called themselves developers. The other view is that teams get smaller because one person can do what used to take five. I actually think both are true at the same time, and the net effect depends a lot on which part of the industry you're looking at. But I'm fairly confident that "developer" in 2030 means something pretty different from what it meant in 2020.

r001.rationale: The candidate says engineers at companies using AI are already not typing most of the code and that agents do the keystrokes, with implementation becoming dramatically cheaper. This communicates that AI systems will produce the vast majority of code.

r002.rationale: The candidate describes engineers specifying what they want built and says the bottleneck is shifting toward clearly specifying desired functionality for agents to implement.

r003.rationale: The candidate identifies evaluating correctness, verification, testing, and reviewing AI output as central parts of the engineer’s role.

astra-6.text:
I think we’re moving toward a world where writing code is a much smaller part of developing software. You’ll spend more time specifying what you want, giving the system the right context, and figuring out whether what it built actually solves the problem.

And that last part is really important. Generating an implementation is one thing. Knowing that it behaves correctly, fits into an existing system, and is something you can maintain is a different challenge. As code gets cheaper to produce, those questions become more central to the engineer’s job.

So I don’t think the change is just that every developer types faster. I think the workflow changes. You can explore more approaches, build things you wouldn’t previously have had time to build, and delegate larger pieces of work. But you still need a way to check that work. The extent to which we can make that feedback reliable will determine how much autonomy these systems can have.

r001.rationale: The candidate says writing code will become a much smaller part of development, but does not predict that AI systems will write the vast majority of software code.

r002.rationale: It says developers will spend more time specifying what they want the system to build, clearly describing a shift toward specifying functionality for AI implementation.

r003.rationale: It identifies checking whether generated work behaves correctly, fits existing systems, and is maintainable as increasingly central to engineers’ work.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the biggest change is that developers will spend less time writing individual lines of code and more time specifying what they want, giving the system the right context, and evaluating whether what it produced actually works.

But writing code is only one part of developing software. You still have to figure out what problem you're solving, understand the constraints of an existing system, and decide what good looks like. If generating an implementation gets much cheaper, those other activities become a bigger part of the job.

So I expect the work to become more iterative. You ask for something, inspect the result, run tests, and refine it. The interesting question is how much of that loop the AI can reliably take on. Getting a plausible first version is useful, but getting something you can trust in production requires feedback and verification. I think building that feedback loop will be a really important part of how software teams work.

r001.rationale: It predicts developers will spend less time writing lines of code, but does not say AI systems will write the vast majority of software code.

r002.rationale: It says developers will increasingly specify what they want and give AI context, while the system generates an implementation.

r003.rationale: It describes inspecting results, testing, refining, and verifying AI output as important parts of development.
